description: Eight factors shaping sport's popularity in the UK, plus how padel and pickleball are growing.
content_html:
Why Are Some Sports More Popular Than Others?

Sport does not become popular by accident. The sports millions of people play and watch — football, tennis, athletics — are popular because a combination of factors has come together over many decades. Understanding these factors helps explain why some sports thrive while others struggle to find participants, and why new sports can suddenly break through. There are eight key factors that drive the popularity of sport in the UK.

Key Fact

The eight factors affecting the popularity of sport are: number of people participating, provision of facilities, environment and climate, live spectator opportunities, media coverage and range, high-level success of national teams or athletes, positive role models, and social acceptability.

Participation Numbers and Facilities

Sports with large numbers of participants generate income through club fees, kit sales and lottery funding — which in turn funds more facilities, coaching and development. It is a positive cycle: the more people play, the better the infrastructure becomes, which attracts even more players. Football has over 11 million registered adult participants in England, making it by far the most played team sport and explaining why there are far more grass pitches per square kilometre than tennis courts.

Provision of facilities is closely linked to participation. If there is no swimming pool within 10 miles, swimming participation will be low in that area regardless of other factors. The closure of public swimming pools in the 2010s led to measurable drops in adult swimming participation in those communities.

Environment and Climate

The UK’s mild, wet climate favours some sports and hinders others. Outdoor cricket requires dry summers; the British weather limits the playing season and discourages casual participation. Winter sports such as skiing need consistent snowfall — which is why the UK produces far fewer elite skiers than alpine nations. Conversely, the UK’s coastline and tidal rivers support a healthy sailing and rowing culture. Climate is not destiny, but it shapes which sports are practical to participate in without expensive facilities.

Being able to watch sport live — at a stadium, an athletics track, or a community pitch — creates emotional attachment and interest that drives participation. A child who attends a Premier League match is more likely to join a local football club than a child who has only watched from home. Premier League stadia regularly sell out at 50,000-plus capacity; the spectator culture this creates sustains grassroots interest.

Media coverage is perhaps the most powerful driver of popularity in the modern era. A sport broadcast on free-to-air television reaches tens of millions of viewers; one locked behind a subscription paywall reaches far fewer. The BBC’s coverage of Wimbledon annually peaks at around 9 million viewers and produces a documented spike in junior tennis sign-ups. The range of sports covered matters too: if a sport appears only once every four years (e.g. at the Olympics), it struggles to build sustained public awareness compared with a sport on television 38 weekends a year.

High-Level Success and Positive Role Models

When elite British athletes succeed on the world stage, participation tends to follow. Swimming participation in the UK rose noticeably after the 2012 Olympics — the “Ellie Simmonds effect” was cited by disability sport organisations as a factor in junior para-swimming club sign-ups. Similarly, Emma Raducanu’s 2021 US Open victory produced a 46% increase in tennis court bookings in the following months. Positive role models make sport feel aspirational and achievable, particularly for young people and for user groups who rarely see someone like them succeeding.

Key Fact

High-level sporting success creates what commentators call the ‘golden generation effect’ — a surge in grassroots participation after elite success. British Cycling’s dominance at the 2012 and 2016 Olympics correlated with a decade-long increase in recreational cycling across all age groups.

Social Acceptability

Social acceptability describes whether a sport is seen as normal, respectable and appropriate for different groups in a given culture. Historically, some sports were considered “not for women” (boxing, rugby) or “too aggressive for respectable families” (martial arts). Cultural shifts, growing media representation, and campaigns like the Rugby Football Union’s “She’s Got Game” initiative have changed these perceptions. Social media has accelerated this: when a sport looks fun and accessible online, social acceptability rises rapidly, particularly among teenagers.

Emerging Sports: What Are They?

An emerging sport is one that is new or rapidly growing in the UK and has not yet achieved mainstream status. Emerging sports typically have a small but enthusiastic participant base, limited facility provision, and are working to establish a national governing body. They often begin as recreational activities before formalising rules and competition structures. The pathway from emerging sport to established sport can take decades — or it can happen very quickly when social media amplifies the sport’s appeal.

Padel: Fast-Growing on UK Courts

Padel is a racket sport played in pairs on an enclosed glass-walled court about a third of the size of a tennis court. It originated in Mexico in the 1960s and became enormous in Spain and Latin America before spreading to the UK. Padel is easier to learn than tennis — the walls mean the ball stays in play longer, so beginners enjoy longer rallies — and it is intensely social. The UK had fewer than 100 padel courts in 2021; by 2025 that number had exceeded 1,000. Padel England secured recognition as the national governing body and affiliated to the Lawn Tennis Association for development support.

Pickleball combines elements of tennis, badminton and table tennis on a smaller court, played with a perforated plastic ball and solid paddles. It is particularly popular with retired people and older adults because the court is smaller, the pace is lower than tennis, and rallies are longer. In 2024, Sport England formally recognised Pickleball England as the sport’s national governing body — a key step in gaining access to lottery funding and local authority facility time. The number of registered pickleball players in England nearly doubled year-on-year between 2023 and 2025.

The factors driving pickleball’s emergence in the UK mirror those for any new sport: low initial cost (courts can be temporarily marked on any hard surface), easy-to-learn rules, high social enjoyment, and growing media coverage on YouTube and social platforms rather than traditional TV.

Not every new sport gains traction. Sports that require expensive specialist equipment, cannot be played in existing facilities, or have rules that are difficult to explain quickly often fail to grow beyond a niche. The absence of a governing body also limits growth — without official recognition, a sport cannot access lottery funding, government facility time, or schools programmes. Social media interest that does not convert to regular, in-person participation also fades quickly. The difference between an emerging sport and a short-lived trend often comes down to whether a committed volunteer community forms clubs, runs competitions, and lobbies for facility access.
exam_tip_html: For questions about popularity factors, name the specific factor (e.g. ‘media coverage’) and then explain how it increases or decreases participation — not just that it ‘makes sport more popular’. For emerging sports questions, use current named examples: padel and pickleball are both recognised by Sport England. Avoid older examples like ‘snowboarding’ which is now well established, not emerging. If you are asked to ‘discuss’ an emerging sport, consider both why it is growing and what challenges it still faces.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Eight factors drive sport popularity: participation numbers, facilities, climate, live spectator opportunities, media coverage, high-level success, positive role models, and social acceptability — learn all eight with one example each.
  • Padel and pickleball are the UK’s leading emerging sports in 2024–25, both gaining national governing body recognition and growing rapidly in club numbers.
  • Emerging sports need a national governing body, facility access, easy rules and a social media presence to move from trend to established sport.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes an 'emerging sport'?
A) A sport that has been established for over 50 years
B) A sport that is new or rapidly growing, seeking to establish clubs and competition structures
C) A sport that only elite athletes can participate in
D) A sport played outdoors only
practice_questions.marks: B) A sport that is new or rapidly growing, seeking to establish clubs and competition structures [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two factors that influence the popularity of a sport in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any two correct factors from: number of people participating / provision of facilities / environment and climate / live spectator opportunities / media coverage and range / high-level success / positive role models / social acceptability. (Both must be named to earn the mark; one alone scores 0.) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain how media coverage can affect the popularity of a sport.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. 1 mark for a basic point (e.g. 'media coverage increases the number of people who know about a sport'). 2 marks for development (e.g. 'when a sport is broadcast on free-to-air television, millions of viewers become familiar with it, making them more likely to want to try it'). 3 marks for a further developed point with a specific example (e.g. add 'the BBC's Wimbledon coverage reaches around 9 million viewers and produces a documented spike in junior tennis sign-ups in the weeks after the tournament'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'social acceptability' in sport and give one example of how changing social acceptability has affected a sport's popularity.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): social acceptability refers to whether a sport is seen as normal, respectable and suitable for different groups in society, including particular genders, age groups or cultures (2 marks for a clear definition; 1 mark for a basic statement).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, women's boxing was seen as socially unacceptable for much of the 20th century; changing attitudes and its inclusion at the Olympics from 2012 onward gradually made it acceptable and led to significant growth in female boxing participation (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague reference). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Keston Racquets Club is considering adding a padel court to its facilities. The club secretary believes padel could grow membership significantly within three years.

Discuss the factors that could affect whether padel increases in popularity at Keston Racquets Club and in the wider UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two factors on each side. For example, factors supporting growth: easy to learn, social, growing media coverage, Sport England investment in facilities; factors that could limit growth: high cost of building a padel court, limited coaching availability, public unfamiliarity with the rules, competition from established racket sports. Both sides are clearly developed and applied to the scenario.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two or more relevant factors with some development, but balance may be uneven.
Developing (2 marks): One or two points with limited development.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Harrow Vale Leisure Trust is writing a report on why swimming is one of the most popular sports in the UK, while volleyball remains much less popular despite being an Olympic sport. The trust wants to use the report to make decisions about facility investment.

Evaluate the factors that explain why participation rates differ so much between swimming and volleyball in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A structured evaluation that addresses multiple popularity factors and applies them to both sports. Strong answers will note that swimming benefits from dedicated facility provision (public pools), year-round indoor participation, strong school curriculum presence, and visible elite success (Paralympic gold medals); while volleyball lacks dedicated facilities (shares sports halls with other sports), has limited free-to-air TV coverage, few nationally recognised British role models, and lower social acceptability as a recreational activity compared to swimming. The answer considers whether facility provision or media coverage is the most significant factor with a clear, substantiated judgement.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two popularity factors applied to both sports with some judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Factors identified for one sport only, or applied without comparing the two sports.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about popularity with no comparison or judgement. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is one of the eight factors affecting sport popularity in the UK?
options: Number of Olympic medals won historically

knowledge_checks.q: Sport England formally recognised which body as the national governing body for pickleball in England in 2024?
Padel is played in pairs on an enclosed _____ court, making it easier to learn than tennis because the ball stays in play longer.
A sport that is new or rapidly growing in a country and is seeking to establish clubs and competitive structures is called an _____ sport.
Match each popularity factor to the correct description.
right: Whether a sport is seen as appropriate and normal in society
High-profile athletes who inspire others to participate
The number and quality of venues available to the public

flashcard_questions.q: How many factors affect the popularity of a sport in the UK?
What does 'provision of facilities' mean in relation to sport popularity?
flashcard_questions.a: The number and quality of sports venues and equipment available to the public.

flashcard_questions.q: Which UK sporting success correlated with a decade-long rise in recreational cycling?
flashcard_questions.a: British Cycling's dominance at the 2012 and 2016 Olympic Games.

flashcard_questions.q: What sport uses a perforated plastic ball and solid paddles on a small court?
In which year did Sport England recognise Pickleball England as the sport's national governing body?
In which country was padel originally invented in the 1960s?
What is the 'golden generation effect' in sport?
flashcard_questions.a: A surge in grassroots participation that follows elite sporting success.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the UK produce fewer elite skiers than alpine nations?
flashcard_questions.a: The UK's climate lacks consistent snowfall needed to support outdoor skiing.

flashcard_questions.q: An emerging sport is one that is new or _____ in a country and has not yet achieved mainstream status.
What is 'social acceptability' in relation to sport popularity?
flashcard_questions.a: Whether a sport is seen as normal and appropriate for different groups in society.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one reason padel is particularly easy for beginners to enjoy?
flashcard_questions.a: The glass walls keep the ball in play longer, producing longer rallies.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is having a national governing body important for an emerging sport?
flashcard_questions.a: It gives access to lottery funding, government facility time and schools programmes.

glossary_terms.definition: The extent to which a sport has participants, spectators, media coverage and cultural recognition in a given country.
The number and quality of sports venues, pitches, pools and equipment available to the public in a given area.
High-profile athletes or sporting figures who inspire others to participate by demonstrating that success is achievable.
A sport that is new or rapidly growing in a country, often supported by a newly recognised national governing body, and that is seeking to establish facilities, clubs and competitive structures.
